docs.text: A blazing-fast, sustainable bioinformatics toolkit written in Rust — for microbial genomics research, and optimised for functions used in data exploration.

docs.title: Formats & Parsing
docs.text:
File types and Parsing behaviour

Genbank (.gbk) & Embl (.embl) GenBank and EMBL are structured plain-text formats for annotated nucleotide sequences. While syntax differs, microBioRust parses both and supports converting either format to GFF3.

Structure and Parsing

Top Level is the Records type. Each genome file has only one top level Records type. Macros have getters and setters for the data, these are SourceAttributes, FeatureAttributes, NonCodingAttributes and SequenceAttributes.

At the next level is the Record type. There may be one or many Record in a Records (up to ~ 2000 but more usually ~ 50 in a Bacterial genome). Each Record holds the DNA sequence which is calculated on the fly by slicing the total sequence of Records with the start and stop coordinates. Each Record also holds the contig's id, nucleotide sequence, coordinates, and four typed attribute builders backed by macro-generated getters (get_) and setters (set_)

  1. source_map (SourceAttributeBuilder $\rightarrow$ SourceAttributes): Record-level metadata (organism, mol_type, strain, db_xref, etc.) and the total start and stop coordinates of the contig sequence
  2. cds (FeatureAttributeBuilder $\rightarrow$ 2. FeatureAttributes): Per-CDS annotation metadata (gene, product, start, stop, strand, codon_start, transl_table), keys are the locus_tag
  3. nc_features (NonCodingAttributeBuilder $\rightarrow$ NonCodingAttributes): Non-coding genomic features (rRNA, tRNA, tmRNA, ncRNA, misc_RNA, regulatory, repeat_region, mobile_element, misc_feature), keys are feature_id
  4. seq_features (SequenceAttributeBuilder $\rightarrow$ SequenceAttributes): Per-CDS nucleotide (.ffn) and translated protein (.faa) sequences, keys are the locus_tag.

The full structure of the SourceAttributes, FeatureAttributes and SequenceAttributes is:

docs.title: Attribute Structs & Supporting Types
docs.text:
RangeValue Sequence coordinates use RangeValue to capture exact positions as well as partial/truncated boundaries (common at the start and end of contigs): RangeValue can be either < value, > value or most commonly Exact value Most RangeValues are Exact(value) with exceptions usually at the start and end of sequences, indicating that they are truncated.

pub enum RangeValue {
    Exact(u32),
    LessThan(u32),    // e.g., <1 (5' partial)
    GreaterThan(u32), // e.g., >500 (3' partial)
}

SourceAttributes stores record-level metadata from top level record source_map (accessed via record.source_map.get_organism(key), record.source_map.get_start(key), etc.). Note that start and stop here refer to the entire record/contig sequence, rather than individual coding sequences:

pub struct SourceAttributes {
    pub start: Option<RangeValue>,
    pub stop: Option<RangeValue>,
    pub organism: Option<String>,
    pub mol_type: Option<String>,
    pub strain: Option<String>,
    pub culture_collection: Option<String>,
    pub type_material: Option<String>,
    pub db_xref: Option<String>,
}

FeatureAttributes

Each Record can have None or many hundreds of coding sequences, CDS (stored in the FeatureAttributes). These are the predicted genes and contain annotation data per gene such as locus_tag (id), gene (may be empty), start, stop, strand (-1 or +1), codon start (1,2 or 3), product.

FeatureAttributes stores the following in an enum:

pub struct FeatureAttributes {
    pub feature_type: Option<FeatureKind>,
    pub start: Option<RangeValue>,
    pub stop: Option<RangeValue>,
    pub gene: Option<String>,
    pub product: Option<String>,
    pub codon_start: Option<u8>,
    pub transl_table: Option<TranslTable>,
    pub strand: Option<i8>,
    // ec_number: Option<String>, // available to enable if needed
}

Gene may be None (if no name has been associated with the cds), strand is either -1 (reverse) or +1 (forward). The codon_start is 1, 2, or 3 (reading frame offset). The transl_table wraps a validated NCBI translation table ID (1..=33). currently EC_number is commented out but could be added back if there is demand

Each CDS also has a DNA sequence .ffn (calculated on the fly from the start, stop and strand) and a protein sequence .faa (translated on the fly from the start, stop, strand and codon_start). The sequences are stored in the SequenceAttributes.

SequenceAttributes stores the following: For each CDS, the coding nucleotide sequence (.ffn) is sliced from the contig sequence using start, stop, and strand, and the protein sequence (.faa) is translated on the fly using codon_start and transl_table. These are stored in record.seq_features

pub struct SequenceAttributes {
    pub start: Option<RangeValue>,
    pub stop: Option<RangeValue>,
    pub sequence_ffn: Option<String>,
    pub sequence_faa: Option<String>,
    pub codon_start: Option<u8>,
    pub strand: Option<i8>,
}

Note the start, stop, strand and codon start of SequenceAttributes and FeatureAttributes are identical Although start, stop, strand, and codon_start match across both structs, storing sequences separately in SequenceAttributes keeps memory layout efficient while allowing sequence slicing/translation and feature metadata queries to run independently without cross-table lookups. Keeping them together may make it easier to slice the sequence and access the specific feature metadata at the same time.

Rust Usage Examples

Parsing GenBank & EMBL with Macros (genbank! / embl!) The genbank! and embl! convenience macros parse a file into a Vec. You can inspect features using either the generated get_* methods or by iterating over the underlying BTreeMap (attributes / seq_attributes / source_attributes): 

use microBioRust::{embl, genbank};

fn main() {
    // Parse a GenBank file (or use embl!("example.embl") for EMBL)
    let records = genbank!("tests/K12_ribo.gbk");

    for record in &records {
        println!("Contig: {} ({} bp)", record.id, record.sequence.len());

        // Inspect source metadata
        if let Some((source_key, src)) = record.source_map.source_attributes.first_key_value() {
            println!("Source: {} | Organism: {:?}", source_key, src.organism);
        }

        // Iterate over all CDS locus tags in sorted order
        for (locus_tag, feat) in &record.cds.attributes {
            // Access fields directly on the FeatureAttributes struct
            // or via generated getters (e.g., record.cds.get_gene(locus_tag))
            println!(
                "{}: gene={:?}, product={:?}, {:?}..{:?} (strand {:?})",
                locus_tag, feat.gene, feat.product, feat.start, feat.stop, feat.strand
            );

            // Retrieve translated protein (.faa) and nucleotide (.ffn) sequences
            if let Some(faa) = record.seq_features.get_sequence_faa(locus_tag) {
                println!(">{}\n{}", locus_tag, faa);
            }
            if let Some(ffn) = record.seq_features.get_sequence_ffn(locus_tag) {
                println!(">{}_cds\n{}", locus_tag, ffn);
            }
        }
    }
}

Streaming Records from Any BufRead Source For streaming large files or parsing in-memory buffers (Cursor), use gbk::Reader (or embl::Reader) with RecordRead:

use microBioRust::gbk::Reader;
use microBioRust::record::{Record, RecordRead};
use std::fs::File;
use std::io::BufReader;

fn stream_gbk(path: &str) -> anyhow::Result<()> {
    let file = File::open(path)?;
    let mut reader = Reader {
        reader: BufReader::new(file),
        line_buffer: String::new(),
    };

    loop {
        let mut record = Record::default();
        reader.read(&mut record)?;
        if record.is_empty() {
            break;
        }
        println!("Loaded {} ({} CDS entries)", record.id, record.cds.attributes.len());
    }

    Ok(())
}

Note on joined CDS features: Multi-exon or spliced features such as join(1..3,10..12) are stored as indexed segment keys (_0, _1, etc.) in both record.cds.attributes and record.seq_features.seq_attributes.

Converting GenBank / EMBL to GFF3

use microBioRust::genbank;
use microBioRust::gbk::gff_write;
use std::collections::BTreeMap;

fn convert_gbk_to_gff(input_path: &str, output_path: &str, include_dna: bool) -> anyhow::Result<()> {
    let records = genbank!(input_path);
    let mut seq_region: BTreeMap<String, (u32, u32)> = BTreeMap::new();
    let mut record_vec = Vec::new();
    let mut offset: u32 = 0;

    for record in records {
        if let Some(ref source) = record.source_map.source_name {
            let start = record.source_map.get_start(source).map_or(0, |v| v.get_value());
            let stop = record.source_map.get_stop(source).map_or(0, |v| v.get_value());

            seq_region.insert(source.to_string(), (start + offset, stop + offset));
            record_vec.push(record);
            offset += stop;
        }
    }

    gff_write(seq_region, record_vec, output_path, include_dna)?;
    Ok(())
}

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
How to Install

Install Rust (recommended method):

Please see here for base environment installation details for Rust programming language

For MacOSX, Linux or other unix OS you can install Rust via:

curl --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 -sSf https://sh.rustup.rs | sh

For further details on Windows please see: other install

Install with Conda: Disclaimer: While conda is a powerful package manager, it is primarily designed for managing Python environments, and the Rust package available may not always be up-to-date or include all the necessary components

conda install conda-forge::rust

Install with Python for Rust with Python InterOp To use Python Interoperability you will need to install Python and additionally you may need (even if in a conda environment):

For Linux: export LD_LIBRARY_PATH=[directory where python is located]

For MacOSX: export DYLD_LIBRARY_PATH=[directory where python is located]

For Windows please see this StackOverflow issue for a fix: fix here and please also see our specific windows_install page

docs.title: Python - microbiorust-py
docs.text:
For ease of use you can call directly from Python

microbiorust-py provides high-performance Python bindings for the microBioRust bioinformatics library via Rust and PyO3. You can call all functions directly from Python—no Rust toolchain required.

No need to install Rust

Install microbiorust-py using pip:

pip install microbiorust

macOS users: If you see a cc linker error or missing libpython when importing, add your Python lib directory to DYLD_LIBRARY_PATH (for example, inside a Conda environment): export DYLD_LIBRARY_PATH=$CONDA_PREFIX/lib:$DYLD_LIBRARY_PATH

Quick Start: GenBank to Protein FASTA All parsed collections are like Python dictionaries (keys(), values(), items(), len(), key indexing, and iteration)

example script for converting from GenBank to protein fasta: 

from microbiorust import gbk_to_faa
result = gbk_to_faa("filename.gbk") 
for entry in result.values():
   print(f">{entry.locus_tag}\n{entry.faa}")

To write FASTA files directly to disk (fastest, with zero Python object conversion overhead), use parse_gbk or parse_embl with .write_faa(), .write_ffn(), or .write_fna():

import microbiorust as mb

records = mb.parse_gbk("filename.gbk")
records.write_faa("proteins.faa")
records.write_ffn("genes.ffn")
records.write_fna("contigs.fna")

Features Overview

Functions can be imported directly from microbiorust or from submodules (gbk, embl, blast, align, seqmetrics)

GenBank Input (microbiorust.gbk) 1. parse_gbk(filename) — parses a GenBank file into a RecordCollection (contig-level records with .features(), .sequences(), .faa(), .ffn(), and .write_*() methods)

  1. gbk_to_faa(filename) — converts GenBank CDS features to a protein FASTA collection (FaaCollection)

  2. gbk_to_ffn(filename) — converts GenBank CDS features to a gene nucleotide FASTA collection (FfnCollection)

  3. gbk_to_fna(filename) — parses GenBank records for DNA sequence contigs (RecordCollection)

  4. gbk_to_gff(filename, dna=False) — converts GenBank format to GFF3 (.gff), optionally appending contig DNA

  5. gbk_to_faa_count(filename) — returns the total count of protein sequences in a GenBank file without allocating sequence strings

    6. Example usages:

    import microbiorust as mb

# Convert GenBank to GFF3 (with DNA sequences included)
mb.gbk_to_gff("genome.gbk", dna=True)

# Count protein CDS entries directly
count = mb.gbk_to_faa_count("genome.gbk")
print(f"Total proteins: {count}")

# Inspect features and sequences per contig record
import microbiorust as mb

records = mb.parse_gbk("genome.gbk")

for contig_id, record in records.items():
    print(f"Contig: {contig_id} ({len(record.sequence())} bp)")

    #iterate over all the annotated features in this record
    for locus_tag, f in record.features().items():
        print(f.locus_tag, f.gene, f.product, f.start, f.stop, f.strand)

    #to look up a specific locus tag directly on the record
    tags = record.locus_tag()
    if tags:
        first_feature = record[tags[0]]
        print("First feature:", first_feature)

    EMBL Input (microbiorust.embl)

    1. parse_embl(filename) — parses an EMBL file into a RecordCollection

    2. embl_to_faa(filename) — converts EMBL CDS features to a protein FASTA collection (FaaCollection)

    3. embl_to_ffn(filename) — converts EMBL CDS features to a gene nucleotide FASTA collection (FfnCollection)

    4. embl_to_fna(filename) — parses EMBL records for DNA sequence contigs (RecordCollection)

    5. embl_to_gff(filename, dna=False) — converts EMBL format to GFF3 (.gff), True/False to append DNA sequence

      Example use:

      from microbiorust.embl import embl_to_faa, embl_to_gff

proteins = embl_to_faa("genome.embl")
for p in proteins.values():
    print(f">{p.locus_tag}\n{p.faa}")

embl_to_gff("genome.embl", dna=False)

      JSON Export JSON Export All collections (RecordCollection, FeatureCollection, SequenceCollection, FaaCollection, FfnCollection) support .to_json() for exporting directly from Rust into a JSON string:

      import json
import microbiorust as mb

records = mb.parse_gbk("genome.gbk")
data = json.loads(records.to_json())

#data is a standard Python dict where the key is the id 
first_id = next(iter(data))
print(json.dumps({first_id: data[first_id]}, indent=2))

      BLAST Input (microbiorust.blast)

      parse_tabular(path) — streaming parser for tabular BLAST output (-outfmt 6), returning a list of hit dictionaries

      parse_xml(path) — streaming parser for BLAST XML output (-outfmt 5), returning nested iteration dictionaries

      Example usage:

      from microbiorust.blast import parse_tabular, parse_xml

hits = parse_tabular("blast_results.tab")
for hit in hits:
    print(hit["qseqid"], hit["sseqid"], hit["pident"], hit["evalue"], hit["bitscore"])

xml_iterations = parse_xml("blast_results.xml")

      Multiple Sequence Alignment (microbiorust.align)

      1. subset_msa_alignment(filename, row_index, col_index) — subsets a DNA or protein FASTA alignment using (start, end) index tuples for rows and columns, returning FASTA-formatted strings

      2. consensus_sequence(filename) — computes a consensus sequence string from a DNA or protein FASTA alignment

      3. purge_gaps(input, output, threshold) — removes alignment columns exceeding a gap fraction threshold (e.g., 0.2) and writes the cleaned FASTA alignment to output

      Example usage:

      from microbiorust.align import consensus_sequence, purge_gaps, subset_msa_alignment

consensus = consensus_sequence("alignment.fasta")
print("Consensus:", consensus)

# Extract rows 0..10 and columns 20..80
subset = subset_msa_alignment("alignment.fasta", row_index=(0, 10), col_index=(20, 80))
for seq in subset:
    print(seq)

# Remove columns with >20% gaps
purge_gaps("alignment.fasta", "filtered_alignment.fasta", threshold=0.2)

      Sequence Metrics (microbiorust.seqmetrics)

      1. hydrophobicity(seq, window_size) — calculates a sliding-window hydrophobicity profile (list[float])

      2. amino_counts(seq) — counts occurrences of each amino acid in the provided sequence (dict[str, int])

      3. amino_percentage(seq) — calculates the percentage of each amino acid in the provided sequence (dict[str, float])

      Example usage:

      from microbiorust.seqmetrics import amino_counts, amino_percentage, hydrophobicity

seq = "MSNTQKKNVPELRFPGFEGEWEEKKLGDLTTKIGSGKTPKGGSENYTNKG"

print(amino_counts(seq))
print(amino_percentage(seq))
print(hydrophobicity(seq, window_size=9))

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
In microBioRust:

You can parse genbank files and save as a GFF (gff3) format as well as extracting DNA sequences, gene DNA sequences (ffn) and protein fasta sequences (faa) Super simple way:

pub fn genbank_to_faa() -> Result<(), anyhow::Error> {
    let args = Arguments::parse();
    let records = genbank!(&args.filename);
    for record in records.iter() {
        for (k, v) in &record.cds.attributes {
            if let Some(seq) = record.seq_features.get_sequence_faa(k) {
                println!(">{}|{}\n{}", &record.id, &k, seq);
            }
        }
    }
    return Ok(());
}

Better for Debugging:

pub fn genbank_to_faa() -> Result<(), anyhow::Error> {
    let args: Vec<String> = env::args().collect();
    let config = Config::new(&args).unwrap_or_else(|err| {
        println!("Problem with parsing file arguments: {}", err);
        process::exit(1);
    });
    let file_gbk = fs::File::open(config.filename)?;
    let mut reader = Reader::new(file_gbk);
    let mut records = reader.records();
    let mut cds_counter: u32 = 0;
    loop {
        //collect from each record advancing on a next record basis, count cds records
        match records.next() {
            Some(Ok(mut record)) => {
                for (k, v) in &record.cds.attributes {
                    match record.seq_features.get_sequence_faa(&k) {
                        Some(value) => {
                            let seq_faa = value.to_string();
                            println!(">{}|{}\n{}", &record.id, &k, seq_faa);
                        }
                        _ => (),
                    };
                }
                cds_counter += 1;
            }
            Some(Err(e)) => {
                println!("Error encountered - an err {:?}", e);
            }
            None => {
                println!("finished iteration");
                break;
            }
        }
    }
    println!("Total records processed: {}", read_counter);
    return Ok(());
}

Example to save a provided multi- or single genbank file as a GFF file (by joining any multi-genbank)

pub fn genbank_to_gff() -> io::Result<()> {
    let args: Vec<String> = env::args().collect();
    let config = Config::new(&args).unwrap_or_else(|err| {
        println!("Problem with parsing file arguments: {}", err);
        process::exit(1);
        });
    let file_gbk = fs::File::open(&config.filename)?;
    let prev_start: u32 = 0;
    let mut prev_end: u32 = 0;
    let mut reader = Reader::new(file_gbk);
    let mut records = reader.records();
    let mut read_counter: u32 = 0;
    let mut seq_region: BTreeMap<String, (u32,u32)> = BTreeMap::new();
    let mut record_vec: Vec<Record> = Vec::new();
    loop {  
        match records.next() {   
            Some(Ok(mut record)) => {
                //println!("next record");
                //println!("Record id: {:?}", record.id);
                let source = record.source_map.source_name.clone().expect("issue collecting source name");
                let beginning = match record.source_map.get_start(&source) {
                                    Some(value) => value.get_value(),
                                    _ => 0,
                                    };
                let ending = match record.source_map.get_stop(&source) {
                                    Some(value) => value.get_value(),
                                    _ => 0,
                                    };
                if ending + prev_end < beginning + prev_end {
                    }
                seq_region.insert(source, (beginning + prev_end, ending + prev_end));
                record_vec.push(record);
                // Add additional fields to print if needed
                read_counter+=1;
                prev_end+=ending; // create the joined record if there are multiple
                },
            Some(Err(e)) => { println!("theres an err {:?}", e); },
                None => {
                println!("finished iteration");
                        break; },
            }
        }
    let output_file = format!("{}.gff", &config.filename);
    gff_write(seq_region.clone(), record_vec, &output_file, true);
    println!("Total records processed: {}", read_counter);
    return Ok(());
}

Example to create a completely new record, use of setters or set_ functionality

To write into GFF format requires gff_write(seq_region, record_vec, filename, true or false)

The seq_region is the region of interest to save with name and DNA coordinates such as seqregion.entry("source_1".to_string(), (1,897))

This makes it possible to save the whole file or to subset it

record_vec is a list of the records. If there is only one record, include this as a vec using vec![record]

The boolean true/false describes whether the DNA sequence should be included in the GFF3 file

To write into genbank format requires gbk_write(seq_region, record_vec, filename), no true or false since genbank format will include the DNA sequence

docs.title: Installation on Windows
docs.text:
Author: Sreeram Peela

Pre-requisites

Rust is the programming language of choice for complex tasks these days. Installing microBioRust in windows requires Rust to be installed and the PATH variables to be added.

We recommend installing Rust (and microBioRust) using Windows Powershell (logged as admin).

Alternately, the latest executables for GUI-based installation can be found here: https://www.rust-lang.org/tools/install

  1. Navigate to the directory of your choice and open Powershell in admin mode.
  2. Download Rust executable from Powershell using the command: 
Invoke-WebRequest
-Uri https://static.rust-lang.org/rustup/dist/x86_64-pc-windows-msvc/rustup-init.exe
-OutFile rustup-init.exe
# Run the below command to start installation
.\rustup-init.exe```

Installing Rust typically can be made through Visual Studio Community installer (Select option 1 when prompted). This documentation is written by selecting this option

Installation VS community installer requires downloading additional packages - Win11_SDK and .. Please note that both these require almost 6GB of memory !!

  1. Select ‘Default installation’ when prompted.
  2. After a typical installation is over, close the powershell and reopen it to make changes in the PATH.

# Check if installation is successful 

cargo help

For a successful installation, the above command will display different options and subcommands in Cargo. We will be using this for installing microBioRust (or any Rust package).

Install microBioRust

The microBioRust repo is being hosted on GitHub here. We recommend using Git for smooth installation. Alternatively, users can download the repo as a ZIP file, uncompress it (with your own choice of tools), and navigate to the directory.

# Clone the repo using Git 

git clone https://github.com/LCrossman/microBioRust.git

# Navigate to the dir 

cd microBioRust

Inside the directory, one can use Cargo to build the library. 

# Inside the project directory
cargo build

The above command downloads and installs necessary dependencies for smooth functioning of the package. Please wait until all the required dependencies are installed and compilation for microBioRust is completed.

Once the package has been built, it is a general practise to test whether installation was successful. For testing the installation, run the command: 

# test installation of the package  
cargo test

The above test instance runs over multiple files packed with the repo, and a final output message can help us in understanding errors. Typically, successful installation gives the following last few lines:

Congratulations!! You have successfully installed microBioRust in your system. You can proceed with Getting started section of the documentation.
